extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom managers, NPR staff, and anyone interested in newsroom ethics policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of NPR's revised newsroom ethics standards governing when and how journalists may participate in public demonstrations, express views on social media, and balance professional impartiality with personal expression. Focuses on who is covered, allowed activities, restrictions, decision processes, and core values the policy lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted expression of democratic, civic values
rubrics_metrics.description: “NPR editorial staff may express support for democratic, civic values that are core to NPR's work, such as, but not limited to: the freedom and dignity of human beings, the rights of a free and independent press, the right to thrive in society without facing discrimination on the basis of race, ethnicity, gender, sexual identity, disability, or religion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy explicitly allows staff to express support for enumerated civic values. This is a carve-out permitting personal expression around human dignity and press freedoms while tying those values to NPR’s mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance at marches, rallies and other public events — limited permission
rubrics_metrics.description: Protests organized with the purpose of demanding equal and fair treatment of people are now permitted, as long as the journalist asking is not covering the event. The policy eliminates the blanket prohibition on participating in “marches, rallies and public events.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include saying 'Black lives matter' or attending a Pride parade in theory allowed, but employees must discuss specific decisions with supervisors. Rallies organized to support a specific piece of legislation or events featuring a slate of political candidates are explicitly off-limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on partisan campaign activity and visible political endorsements
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsroom ethics policies traditionally include prohibitions against putting a campaign sticker on your car or a political sign in your yard (NPR retains these prohibitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some civic advocacy is allowed, visible partisan campaigning or endorsements (signs, stickers, overt support for candidates or legislation at rallies) remain forbidden under the policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism duties override personal advocacy when colleagues are affected
rubrics_metrics.description: When taking a public stance makes it harder for other NPR journalists to do their jobs, there is an expectation that the journalism will take precedence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees must weigh how public participation impacts colleagues’ ability to report; if it impedes colleagues’ work or newsroom operations, professional responsibilities must come first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-based distinctions: reporters vs. commentators
rubrics_metrics.description: “NPR journalists with a role in covering the news should stick to reporting and analysis. Commentators have more leeway to express opinions and may do so as long as they are respectful and grounded in facts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People who report the news are expected to limit public opinion expression to reporting/analysis; commentators and opinion writers have broader latitude but must remain respectful and fact-grounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission for first-person stories by news/programming staff
rubrics_metrics.description: A new addition allows anyone who works in news or programming to publish a first-person story when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicitly expands some kinds of personal expression in bylined first-person pieces, subject to appropriateness standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope/applicability: who must comply
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy refines and narrows the list of staff who are expected to comport with the most restrictive elements of the policy: whether you shape content in any way or hold an executive title. Other job titles (research, archives and data, promotional copy for programming division) are exempt from restrictions on their public behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicability is tied to whether roles shape editorial content or hold executive authority; many behind-the-scenes or promotional roles are not subject to the strictest limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core guiding principles and explicit diversity obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening section lists core values of 'honesty, integrity, independence, accuracy, contextual truth, transparency, respect and fairness' and adds a specific reference to the 'democratic role as watchdogs.' NPR names diversity as a key guiding principle, with a specific obligation to include voices that are routinely left out of the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy anchors permissible behavior to these enumerated values and emphasizes an editorial duty to diverse representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision process: consultation with supervisors and standing committee review
rubrics_metrics.description: The new policy empaneled a standing committee that will review questions and cases, and the policy expects staff to discuss specific decisions with their bosses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment calls around gray-area activities are to be handled collaboratively: immediate supervisors and a standing committee (rather than a single standards editor) will weigh in, providing a process for consistency and appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freelancers and member stations required to follow guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Any freelancer or local journalist whose work airs on NPR is required to follow these guidelines. Additionally, many of the member stations fully adopt NPR's code of ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy’s reach extends beyond directly employed staff to contributors and affiliates whose content airs on NPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refined social media guidance — broader expression with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy updates the section on social media, opening the door for more personal expression while still containing limits; the policy replaces vague language that directed journalists to avoid personally advocating for 'controversial' or 'polarizing' issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy recognizes social media as part of daily workflow and permits expression of core civic values, but past examples (AP firing, newsroom restrictions after tweets) are cited as reminders of consequences for violating policies or creating conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of differential impacts on marginalized journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Black, Hispanic, Asian and Native American journalists have argued that they have been disproportionately confined by — even disciplined over — policies that limit personal expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy revisions are informed by equity concerns: the newsroom must consider how restrictive rules have different effects across staff identities, and the new rules aim to reduce disproportionate constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain impartiality and avoid conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsroom ethics policies traditionally focus on eliminating conflicts of interest by telling journalists what they can't do; the policy retains prohibitions intended to prevent conflicts that would impair impartial coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff should avoid actions that create real or perceived conflicts of interest (e.g., participating in events they would later be asked to cover) and must recuse themselves or refrain from reporting where conflicts exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing vague prohibitions on 'polarizing' topics into concrete rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy removes vague language that directed NPR journalists to avoid personally advocating for 'controversial' or 'polarizing' issues and replaces it with more specific lists and case-by-case guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than blanket prohibitions, the policy provides more explicit permitted and forbidden categories (e.g., human-rights-oriented demonstrations permitted; partisan rallies not permitted) and relies on supervisory review for edge cases.
